World Series. The championship series of Major League Baseball is contested annually between the American League and National League champions. First played in nineteen oh three, it is a best-of-seven competition held in autumn and stands as the defining trophy of professional baseball in North America. Established in nineteen oh three as an annual best-of-seven playoff series between league champions, the format solidified the modern baseball championship and remains the oldest professional sports championship in North America.

Nicknamed the October Classic for its traditional autumn timing, though recent expansions have occasionally pushed games into November, representing baseball's commitment to completion despite weather challenges. The series was suspended during World War One, in nineteen eighteen and nineteen nineteen, and World War Two, in nineteen forty-three and nineteen forty-four, due to wartime priorities, highlighting baseball's role in American civic consciousness during national crises. Games shifted from early afternoon slots to evening broadcasts starting in the nineteen seventies, expanding viewership and making it a primetime spectacle that now reaches global audiences.

The New York Yankees have won more World Series titles than any other franchise, with twenty-seven championships across a century of dominance. Babe Ruth and the Yankees defined the series in the nineteen twenties through nineteen thirties, setting the template for dynasty-building in baseball and establishing the Yankees' cultural identity as a powerhouse franchise. The series has produced iconic moments: walk-off home runs, no-hitters, and individual heroics that define careers and haunt franchises for generations, creating a narrative tradition unmatched in American sports.
